Melanocytic infiltration of the leptomeninges is where the cranial nerves run, and cranial nerve palsy is on the review's list of this disease's neurological manifestations. No cited source shows the infiltrate compressing a nerve, so the edge is drawn through unknown intermediates and could as well run through the raised pressure node.

Profound delay occurs in a minority of children with the lesion and most have none or only mild delay, so this edge asserts a possible consequence and not a usual one. What separates them is partly established: in the largest screened cohort an abnormal scan was the most significant predictor of abnormal neurodevelopment, and the cohort split into intraparenchymal melanosis alone, which was not associated with malignancy or death even when symptomatic, and all other pathology, which was not so benign.

Epilepsy is the commonest neurological manifestation, and in the pooled neurosurgical literature the commonest symptom of any kind. How the melanocytic deposits produce it is not established by any cited source; focal cortical dysplasia in the same patients is one route and the deposits themselves another.

nodes.description: Blocking the pathway the mutation activates. The clinical evidence is case-level: single case reports, one centre's series of four children with NRAS-mutated melanoma of the central nervous system, and a registry study of melanoma of the central nervous system in this disease, none with a controlled comparison. In the series, where three of the four children had congenital naevi, every child improved in symptoms and signs on trametinib for between one and nine months, with no clinically significant side effects and, in one child, stable leptomeningeal disease on MRI at 56 and 139 days; every child then progressed through treatment and died. In the registry study, with published cases added, none of 27 children survived a year, including the nine given trametinib among other treatments, and 14 of the 16 with data had an NRAS alteration. The single patients did not go the same way. One infant's leptomeningeal thickening fell rapidly on trametinib with azacitidine and he was developmentally normal at 53 months. Another child took trametinib for seven months and eventually died of malignant transformation of his leptomeningeal disease. A 13-year-old died five days after binimetinib was started, too soon for a clinical effect, though his tissue showed lower pERK and Ki67 afterwards; the 2014 report calls the drug MEK162, which is binimetinib. A 13-year-old girl with melanosis of the amygdala and medial temporal lobes, seen only on imaging, had no further neurological decline at one-year follow-up, four to five months after trametinib was added to levetiracetam; within about two months of starting trametinib she had a breakthrough seizure-like episode and her levetiracetam dose was raised. Her skin changed in both directions: by her ten-month follow-up, when she had completed 10 weeks of trametinib, the naevus on her forehead had shrunk from 3.1 to 2.7 cm and the borders of her largest naevus looked lighter, while some of her other naevi were reportedly darker. A child with primary diffuse leptomeningeal melanomatosis, an aggressive cancer biologically closely related to this disease, received trametinib and everolimus, followed by nivolumab and ipilimumab with intraventricular chemotherapy; the child improved temporarily and survived seven months, and no part of that result can be attributed to the MEK inhibitor alone.
